passage: Reena pulls her knees up on the bench. 'Anand, can I tell you something weird? Every time Fufaji visits, he hugs me way too long and says, "Give your Fufaji a kiss, na?" Everyone laughs like it's sweet. I used to stand stiff and count till he let go. On Saturday I felt sick before he even arrived. So that night, after he left, I told Mummy. I thought she'd say I was overreacting. She didn't. She sat on my bed and said, "Thank you for telling me. You never have to hug or kiss anyone. Namaste is enough, or a wave." Then she called Papa in, and he said he'd speak to Fufaji himself before the next visit. Next time, I'm doing namaste. From across the room.'

qa.q: What greeting will Reena use next time?
qa.a: Namaste, from across the room.

qa.q: How did Reena feel before Fufaji's visit on Saturday?
qa.a: Reena felt uneasy and full of dread, so much that she felt sick before he even arrived.

qa.q: What did Mummy do right when Reena told her?
qa.a: She believed Reena, thanked her, said no hug or kiss is ever required, offered namaste or a wave, and called Papa in that same night.

qa.q: How might Fufaji see things once Papa speaks to him?
qa.a: Fufaji may feel surprised or embarrassed at first, but can learn that a namaste from Reena is still a respectful, warm greeting.

grounding: Shows a teenager uncomfortable with a relative's long hugs and requested kisses passed off as greeting, whose discomfort is believed and who is told that namaste or a wave is a fine choice.

passage: Jatin here, writing this down because I keep thinking about it. At the Diwali party, Bittu Aunty grabbed my cousin Ojas, fourteen, pulled him into a long squeeze and said, 'Kissi do, na, you've grown so tall!' Everyone laughed. Ojas didn't. He went stiff, looked at the floor, and pulled away the moment he could. I can't know exactly what he felt, but later, on the terrace, he muttered, 'I hate that. Every year.' I asked if I could tell his mum. He shrugged yes. Chachi came up straight away, sat beside him and said, 'You never have to kiss anyone. Namaste is enough. I'll speak to Aunty myself.' Ojas finally looked up.

qa.q: What did Bittu Aunty ask Ojas for?
qa.a: 'Kissi do, na.'

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling while writing this down?
qa.a: Jatin felt uneasy and concerned about Ojas, unable to stop thinking about the moment everyone laughed.

qa.q: What did Chachi do that made a difference?
qa.a: She came straight away, believed Ojas, said namaste is enough, and promised to speak to Bittu Aunty herself.

qa.q: How did Ojas seem to experience the squeeze, from what Jatin saw?
qa.a: Ojas seemed uncomfortable and upset: he went stiff, looked at the floor, pulled away, and later said he hates it every year.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager made uncomfortable by a relative's long hug and demanded kiss as a greeting, whose discomfort is noticed and believed, and who is told namaste is enough.

passage:
"You're hiding in the kitchen again," Tejas said. "Fufaji's asking for you."
"I know." Jaya kept stirring the tea. "He hugs too long. And he always wants a kiss on the cheek. I hate it."
"Then tell Ma. Now. I'll come."
In the corridor Ma listened, glancing toward the drawing room. Jaya's voice shook. "Maybe I'm being dramatic."
"No. If it feels wrong to you, that's enough." Ma squeezed her shoulder. "You can greet him with a namaste. I'll stand right next to you, and if he says anything, I'll handle it."
They walked in together. Jaya folded her hands. "Namaste, Fufaji."
Fufaji opened his arms. Ma stepped in smoothly. "She's doing namaste these days. Come, your tea's getting cold."
After he left, Ma sat with her. "Thank you for telling me. Always tell me."

qa.q: What does Fufaji always want, according to Jaya?
qa.a: He always wants a kiss on the cheek, and he hugs too long.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she said 'Maybe I'm being dramatic'?
qa.a: Jaya felt uncomfortable and anxious, and unsure whether her discomfort would be believed.

qa.q: Which of Ma's steps made Jaya safer?
qa.a: Ma believed her at once, offered namaste as a proper greeting, stood beside her and smoothly stopped the hug, then thanked her for telling.

qa.q: How might Tejas see the choice to go to Ma?
qa.a: Tejas saw that Jaya needed an adult on her side right away, not later, and offered to go along.

grounding: Shows a teenager uncomfortable with a relative's long hugs and kisses, whose discomfort is believed and who is backed in choosing a namaste instead.

passage:
I'm Santosh, and this is about Kavitha Chithi, who I actually love.

Every visit she grabbed me for a hug that went on forever and planted wet kisses on both cheeks, even in front of my friends last Pongal. I'm fourteen. I'd go stiff and count to ten in my head. I told myself it was just her way of saying hello, and that minding it made me ungrateful.

That evening, after my friends had gone, I finally told Amma. I expected, "She's your Chithi, adjust." Instead Amma put down her phone and said, "You don't have to like it. Your body, your choice. Let's tell her together."

She rang Chithi right then, with me sitting there. Chithi was quiet, then said, "Sorry, kanna. High-five from now?"

Now we do a high-five and a namaste. I still get her murukku. I still love her.

qa.q: When did Santosh tell Amma?
qa.a: That evening, after the friends had gone, Santosh finally told Amma.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel during Chithi's long hugs?
qa.a: Santosh felt uncomfortable and stiff, counting to ten, and guilty for minding a loved aunt's affection.

qa.q: Which of Amma's responses helped most, and why?
qa.a: Believing Santosh straight away and calling Chithi together that same evening; it respected the discomfort and fixed it without shaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Kavitha Chithi have felt on the phone call?
qa.a: Chithi was probably surprised and a bit hurt, but quickly said sorry and offered a high-five, showing her love didn't depend on the hugs.

grounding: Shows a teenager uncomfortable with a loving relative's long hugs and kisses, whose discomfort is believed and replaced by another greeting.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday

Karthik (Class 9) came in at lunch with his friend Arnab, who said, "Tell ma'am what you told me." Karthik said that at family functions an older relative insists on kissing him on the cheek and holds him in long hugs, and laughs when he pulls away. "Everyone says it's just affection. Maybe I'm overthinking."

I told him his discomfort is real and worth taking seriously, and that he has every right to greet with a handshake or a namaste instead. We practised: "Namaste. I prefer this."

What I did next: with Karthik's agreement, I phoned his mother before the end of school. She listened and said she would speak to the relative herself before the weekend function. I will check in with Karthik on Monday.

qa.q: Who came in with Karthik?
qa.a: Karthik came in with his friend Arnab.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he said 'Maybe I'm overthinking'?
qa.a: Karthik felt uncomfortable and unsure, doubting his discomfort would be believed when everyone called it affection.

qa.q: Which steps by the counsellor protected Karthik?
qa.a: Believing him, confirming he can choose a handshake or namaste, practising the words, and phoning his mother that same day with his agreement.

qa.q: What was it like for Arnab to bring Karthik in?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt worried for his friend and relieved to hand it to a trusted adult.

grounding: Shows a teenager uneasy about a relative's forced kisses and long hugs, whose discomfort is believed and passed to a parent the same day.

passage:
Sunday night
Verma uncle came for lunch again. Every time, he grabs me in a long hug that doesn't end, squeezes my cheeks and says, "Give uncle a kissie." I'm fourteen. I hate it. My stomach goes tight when I hear his car. Everyone laughs.
Today I stepped back and did namaste instead. He said, "Oho, too big for uncle now?" and pulled me in anyway. My face went hot. Minakshi masi saw my face. She came straight over and said, "Anand does namaste now, Vermaji. That's a lovely greeting." She put her hand on my shoulder and kept it there.
After he left, masi sat with me on the terrace. She said my discomfort is real and I don't owe anyone a hug or a kiss. Then she told Mummy, right then, before dinner. Mummy listened and said, "Next time you do namaste, and I'll stand with you." I felt like I could breathe.
Anand

qa.q: How old is Anand?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: How does Anand feel when Verma uncle arrives?
qa.a: Anand feels uncomfortable and tense, with a tight stomach, hating the long hugs and forced kisses.

qa.q: What did Minakshi masi do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She stepped in immediately, named namaste as a lovely greeting, believed Anand's discomfort and told Mummy the same evening, so Anand had adults on side.

qa.q: How might Verma uncle see his hugs?
qa.a: He probably sees them as affection and doesn't notice Anand's discomfort, which is why he laughed it off.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager uncomfortable with a relative's long hugs and forced kisses, whose discomfort is believed and namaste accepted as a choice.
